title: Adding and Subtracting Large Numbers in Grade 4 (Column Method) + Free Quiz
meta_title: Adding and Subtracting Large Numbers Grade 4 + Quiz
meta_desc: Learn adding and subtracting large numbers in Grade 4: column method, carrying, borrowing across zeros and estimation, with a free quiz and worksheet.
excerpt: By Grade 4 the numbers get long — four, five, even six digits — and the counting tricks that worked earlier fall apart. Here is how I teach column addition and subtraction of large numbers so a child gets the right answer and knows it is right.
author: Sachin Sharma
content:
Give a Grade 4 child a sum like 34,567 + 12,321 and watch what happens. Most reach for the column method they half-remember from Grade 3, then hesitate — do the commas matter? which column do I start from? Adding and subtracting large numbers in Grade 4 is less about new maths and more about one unglamorous skill: lining the digits up correctly by place value and working from right to left without losing track. Get that habit solid and four-, five- and six-digit sums stop being scary. Get it sloppy and even a bright child will be off by a whole thousand.

I have taught this to enough nine-year-olds to know where it goes wrong, and it is almost never the ‘hard’ step. It is a misaligned digit, a forgotten carry, or a borrow across a row of zeros that quietly falls apart. Here is the order I teach it in.

Line up by place value first — always

Before a single digit is added, the numbers must sit one above the other with ones under ones, tens under tens, hundreds under hundreds. This sounds obvious until a child writes 2,450 above 63 and lines the 63 up under the wrong end. The fix is to say it out loud: the last digit of every number is the ones digit, so the right-hand edges line up.

A place-value grid helps enormously in the first week. Draw faint columns headed Th, H, T, O and drop each digit into its box. Once a child can do this without the grid, they are ready for speed.

Carrying in addition

Column addition of large numbers works exactly like it did with small ones — you just do it more times. Start at the ones, add the column, and if the total is ten or more, write the ones digit and carry the ten into the next column. I tell children to write the little carried 1 above the next column, not in their head, because a carry held in the head is a carry lost.

Take 2,758 + 3,467. Ones: 8 + 7 = 15, write 5 carry 1. Tens: 5 + 6 + 1 = 12, write 2 carry 1. Hundreds: 7 + 4 + 1 = 12, write 2 carry 1. Thousands: 2 + 3 + 1 = 6. Answer 6,225. Four small additions, one clear rule.

Borrowing in subtraction

Subtraction is the same idea in reverse. Start at the ones. If the top digit is smaller than the bottom one, borrow ten from the next column left — that column drops by one, and the current digit gains ten. The trouble in Grade 4 is that the numbers now have several columns, so a child has to keep borrowing calmly down the line rather than panicking at the first one.

Borrowing across zeros

This is the step that separates a confident Grade 4 pupil from a struggling one, and it deserves its own drill. Consider 50,000 − 23,456. You cannot take 6 from 0 in the ones, and the column to the left is also 0, and the next, and the next. The borrow has to travel all the way to the 5. In practice each 0 becomes a 9 as the borrow passes through, and the final 5 becomes 4:

ColumnBeforeAfter the borrow
Ten-thousands54
Thousands09
Hundreds09
Tens09
Ones010

Now subtract normally: 10 − 6 = 4, 9 − 5 = 4, 9 − 4 = 5, 9 − 3 = 6, 4 − 2 = 2. Answer 26,544. Once a child sees that every zero simply turns into a 9, the fear evaporates. Practise 40,003 − 15,678 and 70,000 − 8,241 until it is automatic.

Check with the inverse operation

Here is the habit I wish every child left Grade 4 with: addition and subtraction undo each other, so use one to check the other. If 8,000 − 5,236 = 2,764, then 2,764 + 5,236 should bring you back to 8,000. It does, so the answer stands. For an addition, subtract one of the parts from your total and you should get the other part. This single check catches most carry and borrow slips, and it costs thirty seconds.

Use estimation to judge if the answer is reasonable

Checking with the inverse tells you whether you added correctly. Estimation tells you whether the answer is even in the right ballpark — which catches the disaster where a digit lands in the wrong column. Round each number to the nearest thousand (or ten-thousand) first, add or subtract the rounded numbers in your head, then compare.

  • 6,987 + 3,012 rounds to 7,000 + 3,000 = 10,000, so an answer of 9,999 looks right and an answer of 1,999 does not.
  • 50,000 − 23,456 rounds to 50,000 − 23,000 = 27,000, so 26,544 is sensible.
  • If your neat column answer is nowhere near the estimate, you have almost certainly misaligned a digit — go back and check the place values.

Teaching estimation alongside the exact method feels like extra work, but it is the cheapest insurance there is. A child who estimates first rarely hands in an answer that is out by a factor of ten.

A simple daily routine that works

Ten minutes beats an hour. Two days on carrying additions, two days on plain borrowing, one day purely on borrowing across zeros, and a weekend session mixing all of them where the child must also estimate first and check with the inverse afterwards. That mix — do it, estimate it, check it — is what turns a correct answer into a confident one.

The free quiz below covers exactly what we have worked through: column addition with carrying, subtraction with borrowing across zeros, place-value alignment, estimation and inverse checking. Let your child try all eight, then read the explanations together. questions.explanation: Add each column from the right: 7+1=8, 6+2=8, 5+3=8, 4+2=6, 3+1=4. The sum is 46,888.
Borrow across the zeros: each 0 becomes 9 and the 5 becomes 4. 10−6=4, 9−5=4, 9−4=5, 9−3=6, 4−2=2, giving 26,544.

questions.q: In a column subtraction, from which place do you always start?
questions.explanation: You always begin at the ones (the right-hand column) and work left, so any borrowing is handled in order.

questions.q: Rounding to the nearest thousand, about what is 6,987 + 3,012?
questions.explanation: 6,987 rounds to 7,000 and 3,012 rounds to 3,000, so the answer is about 7,000 + 3,000 = 10,000.

questions.q: To check that 8,000 − 5,236 = 2,764, which addition should give 8,000?
questions.explanation: Subtraction is undone by addition, so add the answer back to what you took away: 2,764 + 5,236 = 8,000.
Line up the digits and add each column: no carries are needed here, so the sum is 357,777.

faq.q: What size numbers do Grade 4 children add and subtract?
faq.a: Grade 4 usually works with numbers up to five or six digits — sums like 34,567 + 12,321 and differences like 50,000 − 23,456. The method is the same column method as before, just with more columns to keep aligned.

faq.q: How do you subtract across several zeros, like 50,000 − 23,456?
faq.a: Borrow from the first non-zero digit on the left. As the borrow travels back, every 0 it passes through becomes a 9 and the leading digit drops by one. Then subtract each column normally — 50,000 − 23,456 = 26,544.

faq.q: Why should my child check answers with the opposite operation?
faq.a: Addition and subtraction undo each other, so the inverse is a built-in checker. If 8,000 − 5,236 = 2,764, then 2,764 + 5,236 must equal 8,000. This 30-second check catches most carry and borrow mistakes.

faq.q: How does estimation help with large-number sums?
faq.a: Rounding each number to the nearest thousand and adding in your head gives a rough answer to compare against. If the exact answer is far from the estimate, a digit is almost certainly in the wrong column — a fast way to spot big errors.
